checks.item: Limits so the form and the link cannot flood operators or an inbox, without locking out a legitimate person
checks.evidence: probe1.ts (B): Amy, signed in under her confirmed address, has one request on which we asked her a question. A stranger types her address into the form from 4 devices (8 an hour each): 29 requests accepted, then 429. Amy now has 32 emails from us, and every door is shut for her for 24 hours with 'We already have a lot of messages from this address': a new request while signed in (429), her answer to OUR question through the private link (429), the same through Your requests (429). Her request stays 'waiting'. probe4.ts (5): each stranger-typed request can bring the address three emails (acknowledgement, late notice, closed-without-answer note), so up to about 90 a day. probe2.ts (X): the stranger also learns how much the owner wrote today (owner wrote 12, stranger was stopped after 18).
checks.still_broken: The one counter (30 a day per address) mixes what anyone typed with what the proven owner writes, so it is both a flood allowance against a stranger's inbox and a switch that turns a customer's support off. The limits per request (10) and per device (8 an hour, 30 an hour, 120 an hour) hold as written.
checks.suggested_fix: Count requests typed by someone who is not known to own the address on their own, with a small cap (for example 3 a day and 3 open at once per address), and send one acknowledgement per address per few hours for those. Never count them against messages from the owner (signed in under the confirmed address, or through the link), and never refuse a reply to a question of ours for this reason.

checks.still_broken: One request per address tells an outsider whether that address has written to support in the last 90 days (6 guesses an hour per device).
checks.suggested_fix: Answer first and send afterwards: record the email as queued and let the timer deliver it, or start sendMail without awaiting it (catching its error), so both cases take the same time.

checks.item: POST /public/support/find cannot be used to flood an inbox

new_bugs.title: A stranger can switch off a customer's support for the day and fill their inbox
new_bugs.where: src/server/routes-support.ts: fromAddress() and its two uses (POST /public/support, customerReply)
new_bugs.detail: Steps: Amy is signed in under her confirmed address and has a request on which an operator asked her a question. From 4 device addresses, post {email:'amy@cust.test', message:'filler filler filler filler'} to /api/public/support 8 times each. Result: 29 are accepted, Amy receives 29 acknowledgements (32 emails from us in all), and then for 24 hours Amy gets 429 'We already have a lot of messages from this address...' on a new request while signed in, on her answer to our question through the private link, and on the same through Your requests. Each of the 29 can also bring her a late notice and a closed-without-answer note. Probe: tests/out/verify-support/probe1.ts (B), probe4.ts (5). Fix: count requests from unknown writers separately with a small cap per address (per day and open at once), fold their acknowledgements into one email per few hours, and never count them against the proven owner or refuse an answer to our own question.

new_bugs.title: 'Send me the links again' answers 250 times slower for an address that has written to us
new_bugs.where: src/server/routes-support.ts: route POST /public/support/find (await sendMail only when something was found)
new_bugs.detail: Steps: run the server with a mail server that takes 250 ms per message (local stand-in, tests/out/verify-support/probe3.ts). Post six addresses that have a request and six that have none. Result: 257 to 264 ms against 1 ms, same body {ok:true}. So the form does tell who has written to us. Fix: answer before sending (queue the row for the timer, or do not await sendMail).

new_bugs.title: An API key, or a cross-site post with a session, files a request marked as written by the signed-in owner
new_bugs.where: src/server/routes-support.ts: POST /public/support (known = c.user.email_verified && sameEmail); src/server/router.ts skips the Origin check for public routes
new_bugs.detail: Steps: create a send-scope key, post {topic:'billing', message:'please move my plan to another card and refund the last payment'} to /api/public/support with only the Authorization header. Result: 200, verified=1, operator view written='own' ('Written by someone signed in under this address, which they have confirmed'), first message 'written while signed in', words mailed back. Second: the same route with a session cookie, Origin https://evil.example and content-type text/plain also gives 200 and verified=1, where a signed-in route gives 403. Probes: probe1.ts (A), probe4.ts (2). Fix: treat via 'api_key' as not signed in on this route (or 403), and run the Origin check whenever a session is used on it.

new_bugs.title: An alert with no account shows the first operator's own workspace as the account it is about, with a Trust button
new_bugs.detail: Steps: let the payment code file an alert that has no account (a paid invoice naming an unknown account). Open it as an operator. Result: the request view returns account {name: "Maya Okafor's workspace", via:'address'} because the alert is filed under the first address in OPERATOR_EMAILS and the code looks up the account owned by the login under the request's address. The screen reads 'Account Maya's workspace (owned by the login under this address) · free plan · ... Trust this account' (screenshot shots/op-alert-desk.png). An operator can trust, or misjudge, the wrong account. An alert that does have an account is labelled 'the one this was written from'. Probe: probe1.ts (C), drive2.cjs (4). Fix: for an alert use only its account_id, show no login, and word it 'the account this alert is about'.

new_bugs.title: A request written under another person's address is deleted with the writer's account, and that person is told they closed an account
new_bugs.where: src/server/routes-trust.ts purgeUser (matches by user_id, then sets forget=1); src/server/routes-support.ts FORGOTTEN text and forgetNow
new_bugs.detail: Steps: Eve, signed in, writes under bea@cust.test. An operator asks Bea a question; Bea answers through the private link from her mailbox. Eve deletes her login. An operator answers. Result: the request was marked forget=1 at Eve's deletion; the answer email to Bea ends 'You closed your Sign&Grow account while this request was open. Now that it is answered we have deleted it', Bea's link gives 404 and the request with her words is gone. Had it been answered already, it would have been deleted at once. Probe: probe1.ts (E). Fix: in purgeUser, for rows matched only by user_id (the address is not the deleted login's confirmed address) just clear user_id and account_id and leave the request to the mailbox it belongs to.

new_bugs.title: The operator is told the customer has the answer when the mail server refused it, and nobody hears when it is given up
new_bugs.where: src/server/routes-support.ts: mail() ignores what sendMail returns; src/app/app/operator/tickets.tsx: 'Sent. The customer has it by email.'
new_bugs.detail: Steps: a request from a mistyped address, mail server answers 550 to it, operator sends an answer. Result: 200, status 'answered', first_reply_at set (it counts in the published median), the email row is 'failed' with the server's words, nothing in the request's history says so, and the screen's message is fixed text. No listener records the outcome for help emails, so after the last retry nobody is told. For a request kept after account deletion the request is deleted while the answer has not left. Probe: probe3.ts (b, b2). Fix: use sendMail's status in the answer to the operator and in the history line, register onMailOutcome for these emails (history line and an email to the owner when given up), and delete a forgotten request only once its answer email is 'sent'.

new_bugs.title: A long name or address is cut off in the operator queue, and the address is shown nowhere else
new_bugs.detail: Steps: post a request with a 70 character name and a 150 character address, open /app/operator, filter All, at 390x844 and at 1280x900. Result: the bold heading does not wrap; it runs to x=1176 (phone) and x=1426 (desktop) and is clipped by the card. The opened request shows no address. Screenshots shots/op-queue-all-phone.png, shots/op-queue-all-desk.png. Fix: overflow-wrap:anywhere and min-width:0 on the heading, and print the address in the opened request.

doubts_about_outside_services: Mail server timing: I am fairly sure the find timing gap exists on any real set-up, because the route awaits the hand-over and a real hand-over takes from about 100 ms to seconds. I measured it only against a local stand-in on 127.0.0.1, not a real provider.

Refused mail: most real mail providers accept a message and bounce it later. Then the row says 'sent' and the support code never learns that an answer bounced. I could not see how src/server/bounces.ts is wired to help emails; I am unsure, leaning to 'the operator is never told'.

Header injection: line breaks typed into the form reach the stored subject of the operator email. I ran that subject through the real nodemailer library with its stream transport (no network): it flattens them and no Bcc header appears. Fairly sure this is safe as long as nodemailer is the only way mail leaves.

Device address behind a proxy: every per-device limit (8 requests an hour, 6 finds an hour, 120 link opens an hour) uses the entry of X-Forwarded-For that TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS points at (default 1, the right-most). If the host adds more than one hop (a CDN in front of the platform's own proxy), every visitor may share one address and 8 requests an hour would be the limit for the whole world; with no proxy in front, a caller can type any address and has no per-device limit at all. I cannot see the real host's headers, so I am unsure which applies.

Limits kept in memory: find's 3 a day per address and 6 an hour per device are lost on every restart or deploy and are per process. On a host that restarts or sleeps often the real cap is higher than stated. Sure of the mechanism (rateLimit in util.ts), unsure how often the real host restarts.

Cross-site post: the session cookie is SameSite=Lax, which a browser does not send on a POST from another site, so the public form's missing Origin check is only reachable from a page on a sibling subdomain of the same registered domain. Whether such a page can exist depends on where the product is hosted, which I cannot check.

The private link depends on the server secret (APP_SECRET, or a file in DATA_DIR). If a deploy ever starts with a new secret, every link already emailed stops opening, and find would then send new ones. I cannot check how the real host keeps that secret.

doubts_about_outside_services: Google hd: Google's own guidance treats email_verified plus a gmail.com address, or the presence of hd, as Google being authoritative for the address. I am fairly sure (about 80%) that a Workspace or Cloud Identity address is always in a domain that org verified, so the hd-mismatch case should not occur with real tokens. There have been public reports of Workspace sign-ups usable before domain verification, but I cannot confirm whether hd was ever issued then. I cannot call Google.

Microsoft xms_edov: I am moderately sure (about 70%) that it is an optional ID-token claim set in Token configuration or the manifest's optionalClaims, and that Microsoft omits unverified email claims by default for newer multi-tenant apps. Either way the code fails safe (unvouched means our confirmation email). I do not know whether personal (MSA) accounts ever carry xms_edov:true.

Microsoft key list: apps that use a claims-mapping policy (custom signing keys) must fetch the JWKS with ?appid=<client id>. Optional claims alone do not need this, as far as I know. If an operator adds a claims-mapping policy, every Microsoft sign-in fails with 'failed'.

Endpoints, issuers (accounts.google.com in both spellings; login.microsoftonline.com/{tid}/v2.0, including the personal tenant 9188040d-...), PKCE with a confidential web client, response_mode=query and prompt=select_account all match what I know of both providers (high confidence). Nothing was run against the live providers; my browser run aborted every request that left localhost.

__Host- cookies depend on x-forwarded-proto reaching the app. If a host terminates TLS without sending it, c.secure is false, the server sets sg_signin_note without the prefix, and the landing page (on https) only reads __Host-sg_signin_note, so the first-screen notice (joined, reclaimed, linked) is silently lost. doubts_about_outside_services: Twilio request shape: POST https://api.twilio.com/2010-04-01/Accounts/{AccountSid}/Messages.json, application/x-www-form-urlencoded with To, Body and From or MessagingServiceSid, Basic auth AccountSid:AuthToken, 201 with a JSON sid. This matches Twilio's long-stable Messages API; I am about 90 percent sure, from the documented API, not a live call. API key auth (SK sid + secret) is not supported by this code, which is fine because the settings ask for the account SID and auth token.

Twilio acceptance is not delivery: unassigned numbers, landlines and carrier-filtered messages usually return 201 and fail later (errors 30003, 30005, 30006, 30007) via StatusCallback, which the code never sets. So the app records 'sent' and never tells the sender; the 'I do not get the code' button is the only fallback. About 75 percent sure about which failures surface at API time (21211 invalid format, 21610 opted out, 21408 country not enabled, 21614 not a mobile all come back as 400 and are correctly final).

Duplicates: a 15-second timeout after Twilio actually accepted the message leads to a second send on the timer; the Messages API has no idempotency key. Low cost, same code in both, but counts once in sms_usage and twice on the bill.

Segments: with a 40-character sender name and a normal host the code text is about 180 GSM-7 characters (2 segments); any non-GSM character in the sender's name (for example 'ë', Polish or any CJK) switches to UCS-2 at 70 per segment, 3 or more segments. SMS_DAILY_PER_ACCOUNT counts messages, not segments.

The last line '@host #code' matches the WebOTP / origin-bound one-time code format (must be the last line, host without port), which the code does. Fairly sure; Android Chrome honours it, iOS reads the code from the text anyway.

Generic hook: POST JSON {to, text} with Authorization: Bearer is exactly the contract the brief defines, so it is what an adapter written for it expects. It accepts http:// URLs, which would send the token, numbers and codes in clear text, and any 2xx is taken as sent with no later failure path.

Premium-rate numbers: Twilio blocks premium-rate destinations and limits countries by Geo Permissions by default (fairly sure); a hook provider may not, and this code accepts +1 900, +44 909, +881/+882 and unassigned country codes.

checks.item: 2a. The secret in its three forms, a wrong one, no setting, timing of the comparison
checks.evidence: Probe tests/out/verify-bounces/p4-auth.ts. These answer 200: the query; 'bearer' in lower case; Bearer with a trailing space; Basic with the password and no colon; a wrong query token together with a right Bearer. These answer 401: two token params where the right one is second; the token in another header; the token as the Basic USER name; garbage base64; 'Bearer tsk_abc'. With the setting unset the answer is 404 {error:'Not found'}, the same shape as an unknown route. Both sides are sha256-hashed and then compared with timingSafeEqual on equal-length hex, so the comparison is constant time. A wrong secret is rate-limited per IP and a right one never is.
checks.still_broken: A secret made with `openssl rand -base64` that contains '+' and is pasted raw into ?token= answers 401 for ever, because URLSearchParams decodes '+' as a space (p4: 'base64 secret raw in query' gives 401, percent-encoded gives 200). doubts_about_outside_services: I could not call any provider. Each verdict below comes from my memory of the provider's documented webhook format.

Postmark (fairly sure, about 85%): Bounce webhooks use RecordType 'Bounce' with Type, Email, Details, Description, BouncedAt and Metadata. SpamComplaint and Delivery (Recipient, DeliveredAt, Details) are read from the right fields, and X-PM-Metadata-sg-mail coming back as Metadata['sg-mail'] matches the docs. I am less sure that a send over SMTP to an address Postmark deactivated after a complaint comes back as a ManuallyDeactivated bounce. If it does, the sender is told 'because earlier emails to it came back' when the real reason was a spam complaint, possibly by another account.

SendGrid (sure about the fields, about 90%): event, email, timestamp, sg_event_id, smtp-id, reason/response/status, type 'bounce'|'blocked', and unique_args coming back as top-level keys (sg_mail). I am fairly sure the documented 'dropped' reasons include 'Invalid SMTPAPI header', 'Recipient List over Package Quota', 'Unsubscribed Address' and 'Spam Reporting Address', which makes the always-hard mapping wrong. I am about 60% sure that smtp-id echoes a Message-ID we set over SMTP. sg_mail is the reliable path. SendGrid documents that events are not delivered in order, which makes p2 B realistic.

Mailgun (about 85%): signature plus event-data with event delivered/failed/complained, severity permanent|temporary, delivery-status code/message/description, and user-variables from X-Mailgun-Variables are right. I am not sure Mailgun keeps a Message-ID we set over SMTP. user-variables makes that moot. 'rejected' events are ignored silently.

Resend (about 75%): type email.bounced|complained|delivered|delivery_delayed with data.to as an array and data.bounce {type, subType, message} matches my memory of the 2024 format. Resend webhooks are signed with Svix and that signature is not checked (the token is). With no ids of ours, every Resend event goes through the cross-account address matching shown in p1, so the risk there is near certain on a multi-tenant server.

Amazon SES via SNS (about 90%): the SNS envelope fields, text/plain content type, notificationType/eventType, bouncedRecipients, complainedRecipients, delivery.recipients, deliveryDelay and mail.headers with 'include original headers' are read correctly. I believe SES replaces a Message-ID set by the sender with its own, so commonHeaders.messageId will likely not match ours and X-SG-Mail in mail.headers is the only id. Without that switch on, SES falls back to cross-account address matching. 'OnAccountSuppressionList' can be caused by an earlier complaint, but it is worded as 'came back'.

Whether a stranger can make a customer's mail server hard-reject our email (p1 B, p10) depends on that server's content filter. Rejections with 550 5.7.1 for content are common in corporate filters, but how the provider classifies them (hard or soft) varies: Postmark may call it SpamNotification (soft), and SES often Permanent/General.

overclaims.reality: Copies downloaded while it was still out carry no mark (P8), and the mark can be cropped or lost in a black-and-white copy (probe2).

overclaims.claim: The sender learns 'that you did and when'.
overclaims.reality: The sender also gets the disputer's internet address and full browser string on the envelope page and in the evidence pack (P3).

overclaims.claim: 'We deleted what we knew about it too, so we no longer hold the document, the names on it or its audit trail.'
overclaims.reality: A disputed envelope's operator alert with signer and sender names, emails, title and the disputer's words is kept forever (P5).

overclaims.claim: Only the fingerprint, envelope ID and 'the day it was completed' are kept.
overclaims.reality: completed_at is kept and published to the millisecond (e.g. 2026-11-20T19:37:29.540Z).

overclaims.claim: 'Completed copy opened' marks the first time each person opens the completed copy.
overclaims.reality: For every recipient already in the database the first download after deployment is labelled 'for the first time' whatever they did before (P2).

doubts_about_outside_services: Black-and-white copies: the 50% threshold models a copier, fax or scanner in text or bilevel mode. Many devices in greyscale or photo mode would keep a light grey mark, so I am fairly sure but not certain the mark disappears on real office copiers; the corner crop finding does not depend on any device.
Forwarded completion emails: whether recipients forward them (to a landlord, bank, colleague) is user behaviour I cannot measure; the code in the email is confirmed (P4).

Mail link scanners: 'Completed copy opened' and 'Opened again' can be written by a scanner that runs JavaScript on the /sign page; I could not test a real scanner. The completion email's button points at the page, not the download, which lowers the risk.

The dev server reloaded many times while other engineers edited files (signing page and /check took several tries to render); that looked like work in progress elsewhere, not a fault of this piece. Final passes rendered every screen.
